prompt: What question does a regression test ask of a candidate release?

choices.text: Whether customers will like it
choices.why: That is production's question, after release.

choices.text: Whether its average beats the last release's
choices.why: An average can rise while a case breaks.

choices.text: How fast its model answers
choices.why: Time is reported, not the question.

choices.text: What it changed, case by case
choices.why: Right. Not whether it is good.

prompt: Why do the candidates in releases.json start in 2099?

choices.text: So they are priced at a future price
choices.why: The runs are priced at today's prices.

choices.text: So nothing in production picks them up
choices.why: Right. evalrun.py's --release runs them anyway.

choices.text: Because a release needs a date after the set's
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: So that regress.py sorts them last
choices.why: regress.py takes them by name.

prompt: Match each candidate to what it changes.
Comparing 2026.09.4 with 2026.10.1, how many cases broke?
Why was the floor release cheaper and faster?

choices.text: Its model was a smaller one
choices.why: Both used llama3.2:3b.

choices.text: It cached the replies from the week before
choices.why: There is no cache here.

choices.text: It refused more questions
choices.why: Right. A refusal is short and calls no model: the savings were unanswered questions.

choices.text: The price of llama3.2:3b fell on 30 September
choices.why: Every run is priced at today's prices, so a price change cannot separate them.

prompt: What is the first rule of reading a regression report, from the release that shipped?

choices.text: Read cost and latency beside the broken cases
choices.why: Right. Never instead of them.

choices.text: A faster release is a better release
choices.why: This one was faster because it answered less.

choices.text: Ignore the held-out split until the end
choices.why: True of tuning, not the rule this report teaches.

choices.text: Only a significant p-value counts
choices.why: Seven broken cases at p = 0.18 still block it.

prompt: Which cases did the floor release break? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: e02, who pays for return postage
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: e14, paying in instalments
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: e30, a lost parcel with an order number
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: e12, e-books on a Kindle
choices.why: The floor release fixed that one: with fewer chunks the model answered.

prompt: In a paired comparison, which cases carry the information?

choices.text: The ones both releases got right
choices.why: They say nothing about the difference.

choices.text: The held-out ones
choices.why: Split does not decide it.

choices.text: The ones that changed verdict
choices.why: Right. Agreements say nothing about the difference.

choices.text: The ones with the longest replies
choices.why: Length plays no part.

prompt: Seven changed cases, all broken, as for the smaller model. What is the exact two-sided McNemar p-value?
p = 0.18 for the floor release. Why does it still not ship?

choices.text: Because 0.18 is near enough to 0.05
choices.why: No threshold is being stretched here.

choices.text: Because McNemar is the wrong test
choices.why: It is the right test for paired verdicts.

choices.text: Because the held-out split was not run
choices.why: It was, and it broke one case as well.

choices.text: Seven customer questions broke
choices.why: Right. A broken case is a fact, whatever the p-value.

prompt: Comparing two releases on the same questions, case by case, is called a ___ comparison.
The smaller model is 62% cheaper and 42% faster. Why is it not the release to ship?

choices.text: It broke seven cases and fixed none
choices.why: Right, at p = 0.016, and it broke checks on ten more.

choices.text: Its p-value is above 0.05
choices.why: It is 0.016, the one result in the lesson below 0.05.

choices.text: It writes fewer output tokens
choices.why: It writes 39% more.

choices.text: It costs more per token than llama3.2:3b
choices.why: It costs a third as much.

prompt: 2026.10.4 is 37% cheaper than production. Why ship 2026.10.3 instead?

choices.text: 2026.10.4 breaks seven cases
choices.why: Right. 2026.10.3 fixes seven and breaks two, both named.

choices.text: 2026.10.3 is cheaper than 2026.10.4
choices.why: It costs 50% more than production.

choices.text: 2026.10.4 has a significant p-value
choices.why: Its p is 0.55.

choices.text: llama3.2:1b is not allowed in production
choices.why: No rule says so; the report decides.

prompt: How many replies changed between 2026.10.1 and 2026.10.2, the smaller model?
Why does regress.py count the replies that changed, as well as the verdicts?

choices.text: e31 changed and passed while wrong
choices.why: Right. e31 contradicts its source and passes the facts.

choices.text: Replies are too slow to grade by machine
choices.why: They are graded by machine in the same run.

choices.text: To find out which release wrote each reply
choices.why: Each run already records its release.

choices.text: Because McNemar's test needs that number
choices.why: McNemar uses only the changed verdicts.

prompt: 2026.10.3 has the settings of 2026.09.4, and e31 was answered differently by the two. Why?

choices.text: Temperature 0 is not fully repeatable
choices.why: Right. Near-ties can go either way between runs.

choices.text: The two releases do not have the same floor
choices.why: Both have a floor of 0.4.

choices.text: The set changed between the two runs
choices.why: regress.py would have refused to compare them.

choices.text: Ollama gives each release its own model
choices.why: Both use llama3.2:3b.

prompt: Why did regress.py refuse to compare 2026.10.1 with run v1?

choices.text: v1 used a different release
choices.why: Same release, 2026.10.1.

choices.text: The name v1 is not a release
choices.why: Runs can have any name.

choices.text: v1 asked another set's questions
choices.why: Right. Different questions, no comparison.

choices.text: eval-spans.jsonl was missing
choices.why: It was there.

prompt: Which does a regression test as this lesson builds it report? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Cases broken and fixed, by name
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Checks that newly fail
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Cost and latency with their direction
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether customers will be happier
choices.why: Production answers that.

prompt: A candidate passes the regression test. What has been shown?

choices.text: That it is good
choices.why: Only that it is no worse here.

choices.text: That it is no worse here than production
choices.why: Right. Held-out and production signals come after.

choices.text: That every customer question will be answered
choices.why: The set is 32 questions.

choices.text: That its cost is within budget
choices.why: Only if a budget was set and checked.

prompt: Put these in the order a change meets them.
items: the held-out split, once the candidate is final

prompt: A candidate fixes three cases and breaks one, p = 0.625. What does the team do with the broken one?

choices.text: Ignore it, since fixes outnumber breaks
choices.why: A broken case is read first.

choices.text: Remove it from the set
choices.why: That hides the regression.

choices.text: Wait for a significant p-value
choices.why: Cases are facts, not statistics.

choices.text: Read it, and decide whether it is acceptable
choices.why: Right. It blocks until somebody has.

prompt: Pass rates 25/32 and 20/32 compared as two numbers, with ±15-point intervals. What does a paired test add?

choices.text: It narrows both of the intervals to ±5 points
choices.why: It does not compute intervals at all.

choices.text: It weighs held-out cases twice
choices.why: Every case counts once.

choices.text: It adds the judge's verdicts
choices.why: No judge is involved.

choices.text: It looks only at the nine that changed
choices.why: Right. The 23 unchanged ones say nothing about the difference.
